title: LLD interview tips: method and scoring
scopeHtml: Scope: clarifying requirements, the timed method, naming, extensibility talk and what interviewers score.

notes.title: What an LLD interview really tests
notes.html:
A low-level design (LLD) interview asks you to design classes and their relationships for a small system (parking lot, elevator, LRU cache, splitwise) in about 45 to 60 minutes. It is not about drawing perfect UML. It tests whether you can turn a vague idea into clean, extensible, working code under time pressure.

What the interviewer scores, roughly:

  1. Did you clarify requirements before coding?
  2. Are the entities and responsibilities sensible (SOLID)?
  3. Is it extensible when the next requirement arrives?
  4. Is the code correct, readable and runnable?
  5. Did you handle edge cases and concurrency?
  6. Did you communicate your trade-offs?

Worked example. "Design a parking lot." A weak answer starts typing class ParkingLot at minute 1. A strong answer spends 5 minutes on scope (levels? vehicle types? pricing? entry/exit gates?), 5 on entities, 10 on a class sketch, 20 on core code, 10 on extensions.

Industry examples. Interview loops at Amazon (LLD with Leadership Principles), Uber, Flipkart, Swiggy and Atlassian commonly use machine-coding or LLD rounds; machine-coding rounds ask for runnable code in 90 to 120 minutes with tests.

Everyday analogy. An architect asks the client questions before drawing walls.

Common interview traps.

  • Treating it as a pattern quiz; patterns are tools, not the goal.
  • Silence: the interviewer cannot score what you do not say.

notes.title: Clarifying requirements
notes.html:
Spend the first 5 to 8 minutes asking questions and writing the answers down. Ambiguity is deliberate; the interviewer wants to see you cut scope.

Question buckets:

  • Actors: who uses it (customer, admin, guard)?
  • Core use cases: the 3 to 5 things it must do (park, unpark, find a free spot, pay).
  • Scale and shape: one lot or many? 100 or 100,000 spots? One process or distributed? (LLD is normally single process.)
  • Rules: pricing, limits, priorities, failures (full lot?).
  • Out of scope: payments gateway, UI, persistence. State them so you do not build them.

Then write a short list on the board:

Functional:
  1. Park a vehicle -> returns ticket
  2. Unpark with ticket -> returns fee
  3. Show free spots per type
Non-functional:
  - Thread-safe parking (many gates)
  - Easy to add new vehicle types and pricing rules
Out of scope: payment gateway, UI, DB

Worked example. Asking "single lot, 3 levels, 200 spots per level, cars/bikes/trucks, hourly pricing, multiple gates" fixes the model: 600 spots, 3 spot sizes, pricing strategy, concurrency at the gates. Without it you might build a multi-city system or a single-spot toy.

Industry examples. Amazon bar-raisers explicitly watch whether you "dive deep" only after defining the problem; Google's design interviews grade "handling ambiguity".

Everyday analogy. A tailor measures before cutting cloth.

Common interview traps.

  • Asking 30 questions; ask the 6 that change the design.
  • Not confirming the list back ("so we agree on these 4 use cases?").
  • Starting to code before the interviewer says go.

notes.title: The method with a clock
notes.html:
Use a fixed script so you never freeze. Typical 45-minute budget:

Minutes Step Output
0 to 5 Clarify Requirements list, out-of-scope list
5 to 10 Entities and relationships Nouns become classes, verbs become methods
10 to 18 Class diagram + patterns Interfaces, key relationships, where it varies
18 to 35 Code the core flow Compiles; main flow works
35 to 42 Edge cases, concurrency, tests Named failure modes
42 to 45 Extensions and wrap-up "To add X, I change only Y"

How to find entities: underline the nouns in the requirements (Vehicle, Spot, Ticket, Level), then ask who owns each action. Verbs ("park", "calculate fee") become methods on the entity that has the data.

Requirement noun/verb        ->   Design
Vehicle, Spot, Ticket, Level ->   classes
park(vehicle)                ->   ParkingLot.park
fee(ticket)                  ->   PricingStrategy.fee
vehicle type varies          ->   enum + strategy / subclass

Worked example. At minute 18 you must be typing code. If you are still polishing the diagram, cut it: an interviewer prefers a working simple core over a perfect diagram with no code.

Industry examples. Machine-coding rounds at Flipkart/Swiggy/Razorpay grade "working code, running demo, extensibility" in a fixed time, in that order.

Everyday analogy. A chess clock: the position matters, but you must move.

Common interview traps.

  • Spending 20 minutes on UML.
  • Coding everything before the core flow runs end to end.
  • Skipping the last 3 minutes; the extension discussion often decides the hire/no-hire.

notes.title: Naming and class design
notes.html:
Names carry your design. A good name lets the interviewer read your code without you explaining it.

Rules:

  • Classes are nouns (ParkingSpot, PricingStrategy), methods are verbs (park, calculateFee), booleans read as questions (isFree).
  • Name by role, not by type: FeeCalculator, not Manager/Helper/Util/Data.
  • One class, one reason to change (Single Responsibility). If you need "and" to describe it, split it.
  • Prefer small interfaces named after the capability (Payable, Notifier).
  • Make fields private final unless mutation is the point; expose behavior, not data (tell, do not ask).
  • Use enums for closed sets (VehicleType), strategies for open behavior.
// BEFORE: vague
class Manager { void doIt(int t, int x) { ... } }

// AFTER: intent clear
class FeeCalculator {
    Money calculate(Duration parked, VehicleType type) { ... }
}

Kotlin variant: data class Ticket(val id: String, val spot: Spot, val entry: Instant); sealed interface for closed hierarchies.

Worked example. Level holds its spots and finds a free one (Optional<Spot> findFree(VehicleType)); ParkingLot only picks a level. Each class is 30 to 60 lines, understandable at a glance.

Industry examples. The JDK is a good teacher: Comparator, Executor, Supplier, List are role names; Google Java Style and Effective Java Chapter 4 on class design.

Everyday analogy. Labels on kitchen jars: you never open the wrong one.

Common interview traps.

  • Utils and Manager classes that become dumping grounds.
  • Public mutable fields.
  • Names like data, temp, obj in front of an interviewer.

notes.title: Extensibility talk
notes.html:
Interviewers always ask "what if we add X?". Prepare to answer with: which class changes, which does not. The goal is Open/Closed: extend by adding code, not editing working code.

Pattern for the answer: "Today X is an enum with a switch in one place. If a new type arrives I add a class implementing Y and register it; nothing else changes."

Typical extensions and where to put the seam:

New requirement Seam you prepared
New vehicle type VehicleType enum + SpotSize mapping, or a Vehicle subclass
New pricing rule (weekend, surge) PricingStrategy interface
New payment method PaymentProcessor interface + factory/registry
Notifications on events Observer / listener interface
Persist to a DB Repository interface with an in-memory implementation 
interface PricingStrategy { Money fee(Duration d, VehicleType t); }
class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy { ... }
class WeekendPricing implements PricingStrategy { ... }
class ParkingLot {
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;      // injected, swappable
    ParkingLot(PricingStrategy pricing) { this.pricing = pricing; }
}

Warning: do not build every seam up front. Add seams for the 2 or 3 most likely changes (which the clarifying questions revealed); for the rest, say how you would refactor.

Worked example. Interviewer: "add EV charging spots". Answer: add EV to SpotType, add ChargingSpot carrying charger state, update the spot-selection strategy; Ticket, PricingStrategy, Level stay unchanged. Three edits, no rewrite.

Industry examples. Plugin systems (IntelliJ, VS Code), Spring's strategy beans, Android RecyclerView.Adapter view types are all seams chosen for known variation.

Everyday analogy. Wall sockets: any new appliance fits without rewiring the house.

Common interview traps.

  • Answering "I would rewrite it" or "just add an if".
  • Interfaces for everything; show seams only where change is plausible.
  • Extending by inheritance when composition (strategy) is cleaner.

notes.title: What interviewers score
notes.html:
A typical rubric has 5 to 6 rows, each rated strong / ok / weak. Know it and aim at every row.

Dimension Strong looks like
Requirements Asked focused questions, wrote scope, noted out-of-scope
Modeling Clear entities, right owners of behavior, no god class
Principles and patterns SOLID applied with reason; patterns only where something varies
Code quality Compiles, readable, small methods, validation, meaningful names
Correctness and edge cases Full lot, invalid ticket, double unpark, null inputs
Concurrency Named the shared state and protected it
Communication Thought aloud, stated trade-offs, took hints well

Hint handling matters: if the interviewer asks "what happens if two cars arrive together?", it is a hint to talk about concurrency. Acknowledge, fix, move on; do not argue.

Worked example. Candidate A: perfect Strategy + Factory + Observer, but code does not run, no edge cases. Candidate B: simple, correct, runnable, handles full lot and double unpark, explains how to add pricing. B usually wins.

Industry examples. Amazon scores against Leadership Principles (ownership, dive deep) alongside design; Uber/Atlassian machine-coding rounds also score test coverage and code structure.

Everyday analogy. A driving test: smooth, safe and observant beats flashy.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimizing for fancy patterns over correct code.
  • Ignoring a hint.
  • Not testing your own solution with one worked example (park 3 cars, unpark 1).

notes.title: Communication and recovery
notes.html:
Narrate decisions in one sentence each: choice, reason, alternative. "I use a Map<String, Ticket> for lookup by id, O(1); the alternative is scanning a list, O(n)."

If you get stuck:

  1. Say what you are stuck on ("unsure whether the lot or the level owns spot search").
  2. Choose one, state the trade-off, continue.
  3. Offer to revisit at the end.

If you realize a mistake: say it, fix it quickly; interviewers rate recovery highly.

Do a mini dry run at the end: walk one request through your classes, with real values.

park(car KA-01) -> Level 0 free car spot #12 -> Ticket T-1 (entry 10:00)
unpark(T-1) at 12:30 -> 3 hours (rounded up) x Rs 40 = Rs 120

Industry examples. Google and Meta interview guides repeatedly say "think out loud"; mock-interview platforms like Pramp and interviewing.io grade communication as a separate column.

Everyday analogy. A co-pilot calling out checks so the pilot can trust them.

Common interview traps.

  • Long unexplained pauses.
  • Defending a flawed choice instead of adjusting.
  • Dry running with vague data instead of concrete numbers.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• LLD interviews score: requirements, modeling, principles and patterns, working code, edge cases, concurrency, communication.
  • Clarify first (5 to 8 minutes), write scope and out-of-scope, confirm.
  • Follow a clock: clarify, entities, diagram, code core, edge cases, extend; have code by minute 18.
  • Name by role (nouns for classes, verbs for methods); avoid Manager/Util; one reason to change per class.
  • For extensibility, prepare seams for the 2 or 3 likely changes and say exactly what changes when a new one arrives.
  • Narrate trade-offs, take hints, dry run with real numbers, and prefer simple correct code over pattern decoration.

questions.promptHtml: What is an LLD interview actually testing, and how is it different from a pattern quiz?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Candidates who think it is a UML or pattern test lose points on clarity, working code and extensibility.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It tests whether I can turn a vague idea into clean, extensible, working classes in about 45 to 60 minutes. The interviewer scores clarifying questions, sensible entities and responsibilities, extensibility, correct readable code, edge cases and concurrency, and how I communicate trade-offs. Patterns are tools I use when something varies, not the goal.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Typical flow: clarify, entities, class sketch, code the core, edge cases, extension. A strong candidate starts typing only after minute 5 to 8 and before minute 18 has code. Machine-coding rounds (90 to 120 minutes) additionally expect runnable code and tests.

Clarify -> Entities -> Class diagram -> Code core -> Edge cases -> Extend

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Starting class ParkingLot in minute 1.
  • Treating it as a pattern quiz.
  • Silence: the interviewer cannot score what you do not say.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does a typical rubric include? -> Requirements, modeling, principles/patterns, code quality, correctness, concurrency, communication.
  2. UML needed? -> A rough class sketch, not perfect UML.
  3. What decides hire vs no hire? -> The combination, especially working code plus an extension story.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: names patterns. Senior: describes the scoring axes and manages the clock deliberately.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The same skills show up in design reviews: scoping before building, and stating where the design will bend.

questions.promptHtml: What do you ask in the first minutes of an LLD problem, and how do you avoid asking too much?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Ambiguity is deliberate; they watch whether you cut scope sensibly.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I spend 5 to 8 minutes on a few buckets: actors, the 3 to 5 core use cases, scale and shape, rules (pricing, limits, failures), and out of scope. I ask the roughly six questions that change the design, write the functional and non-functional list on the board, and confirm it back with the interviewer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example for a parking lot: single lot or many, levels and spots count, vehicle types, pricing model, multiple gates (concurrency), payment in scope or not.

Functional: park -> ticket; unpark -> fee; free spots per type
Non-functional: thread-safe gates; easy to add vehicle types and pricing rules
Out of scope: payment gateway, UI, DB

"Single lot, 3 levels, 200 spots per level, cars/bikes/trucks, hourly pricing, multiple gates" fixes the model: 600 spots, 3 spot sizes, a pricing strategy, concurrency at gates.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Asking 30 questions.
  • Not writing the answers down or confirming them.
  • Coding before the interviewer says go.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if the interviewer says "your call"? -> State assumptions explicitly and proceed.
  2. Which question changes the design most? -> Concurrency and extensibility axes.
  3. How do you say out of scope? -> "I will not build payments; I will leave an interface for it."

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: starts coding or asks random questions. Senior asks a focused set, writes the scope and non-goals, and states the assumptions that are decision points.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The same habit prevents building a multi-city system when the stakeholder meant a single site.

questions.contextHtml: The interviewer says only: "Design a food delivery order system." You have 45 minutes. The interviewer is deliberately vague and will answer questions but not volunteer anything. Last candidate spent 15 minutes asking 25 questions and had 10 minutes left to code.
questions.promptHtml: What do you ask and what do you write down? How do you decide when to stop asking?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Starts with class Order, or asks everything about payments, maps and driver routing.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: (a) Actors: customer, restaurant, delivery agent? (b) Core flows: place, accept, assign, deliver, cancel? (c) Is it one process and in-memory (LLD scope)? (d) Pricing: items, tax, discounts? (e) Concurrency: many orders on the same restaurant and one agent assigned once? (f) Out of scope: maps, payments, UI, DB?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A. I set a time box: 6 minutes for scope.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The design axes likely to change: order state machine, agent assignment strategy, pricing rules.
  4. How I'd verify each: Say them aloud: "I will assume order states PLACED, ACCEPTED, PICKED_UP, DELIVERED, CANCELLED; assignment is nearest-free agent; is that right?"
  5. Root cause of failure for others: Treating scope questions as a quiz instead of a funnel.
  6. Fix: Write the list:
Functional: place order, restaurant accepts, assign agent, track state, cancel before pickup
Non-functional: thread-safe assignment, easy new assignment/pricing strategy
Out of scope: payments, maps, notifications, persistence
  1. Prevention: Confirm "agree on these 5 use cases?" then start entities.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not ask about databases or microservices; this is class design.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Interviewer adds "must support scheduled orders" at minute 30? -> Say which class changes (order state plus a scheduler) and keep going.
  • Interviewer refuses to answer? -> Pick an assumption, state it, move on.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite candidate won a loop by stating five assumptions in the first six minutes and sticking to them.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: starts coding or asks 25 questions.
  • Hire: about six focused questions with a written scope.
  • Strong hire: ties questions to design axes, states assumptions and out-of-scope, confirms agreement.

questions.contextHtml: It is minute 22 of a 45-minute round for an elevator system. You have a polished class diagram with 14 classes (Elevator, Floor, Request, Scheduler, Door, Display, Panel, ...) but no code, and you have not decided whether to code. The interviewer glances at the clock.
questions.promptHtml: What do you do in the next minute and how do you use the remaining 23 minutes?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Keeps refining the diagram or tries to code all 14 classes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: "Do you want runnable code for the core flow?" It sets the target.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop the diagram. Say: "I am behind; I will cut to the core: Elevator, Request, Scheduler."
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Which classes are on the main path (request a floor, pick an elevator, move)? Door, Display and Panel can be stubs.
  4. How I'd verify each: Ask what the minimum demo is: "Request(5) -> nearest idle elevator gets it".
  5. Root cause: Over-investing in the diagram; the budget was 8 minutes for design.
  6. Fix: Plan for 23 minutes: 12 minutes code core (Request, Elevator state, a SchedulingStrategy interface and one NearestIdle implementation), 6 minutes edge cases (no elevator, overload) and concurrency, 4 minutes extension (new scheduling strategy).
Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface SchedulingStrategy { Optional<Elevator> pick(List<Elevator> es, Request r); }
class NearestIdle implements SchedulingStrategy {
    public Optional<Elevator> pick(List<Elevator> es, Request r) {
        return es.stream().filter(Elevator::isIdle)
                 .min(Comparator.comparingInt(e -> Math.abs(e.floor() - r.floor())));
    }
}
class NearestIdle : SchedulingStrategy {
    override fun pick(es: List<Elevator>, r: Request) =
        es.filter { it.isIdle }.minByOrNull { abs(it.floor - r.floor) }
}
  1. Prevention: Set checkpoints: code must start by minute 18.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: No attempt to implement all 14 classes; I say what I stubbed.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Interviewer says "skip code, discuss"? -> Switch to extension talk with the diagram.
  • Code does not compile at minute 40? -> Say what is missing, dry run the flow verbally with values.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite candidate with a perfect diagram and no code lost to one with a short working core.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: keeps diagramming.
  • Hire: cuts scope and codes the core.
  • Strong hire: states the cut aloud, keeps a time plan, ends with a dry run and extension.

questions.contextHtml:
A candidate's parking code in a live round:

class Manager {
    public List<Object> data;
    public int t;
    void doIt(int x, int y, boolean b) { ... }
    static Map<String, Object> cache = new HashMap<>();
}

The interviewer asks you, as a mock reviewer, to give feedback and show the rewrite for "park a vehicle and compute the fee".
questions.promptHtml: What do you flag and how do you rewrite it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only renames the variables.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does doIt do: assign a spot or compute a fee? What is t? Who owns the cache?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) role-less Manager is a dumping ground; (b) public mutable fields and static state; (c) boolean and int parameters hide meaning; (d) List<Object> loses types.
  4. How I'd verify each: Try to describe Manager without the word "and"; try to unit test it.
  5. Root cause: Names carry no design, so the structure is not visible.
  6. Fix: Name by role, types and behavior:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class FeeCalculator {
    Money calculate(Duration parked, VehicleType type) { ... }
}
class Level {
    private final List<Spot> spots;
    Optional<Spot> findFree(VehicleType type) { ... }
}
class FeeCalculator { fun calculate(parked: Duration, type: VehicleType): Money = TODO() }
data class Ticket(val id: String, val spot: Spot, val entry: Instant)
  1. Prevention: Private final fields, enums for closed sets, strategies for open behavior; no Util/Manager/Helper.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not over-split into a class per method.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Boolean parameter really needed? -> Replace with two methods or an enum.
  • Where does isFree live? -> On Spot (tell, do not ask).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a Manager with 25 methods took 40 minutes to reason about; five small classes took five minutes each.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: renames only.
  • Hire: role names, private fields, typed parameters.
  • Strong hire: finds static state, explains SRP and testability, shows the rewritten classes.

questions.promptHtml: The interviewer asks "what if we add X?". How do you structure the answer, and where do you place seams without over-engineering?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Open/Closed is the senior signal. They want a precise "this changes, this does not".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I answer with: which class changes, which do not, and why. For example: "Vehicle type is an enum with a mapping in one place; a new type adds one enum value and a mapping, Ticket and Level do not change." I prepare seams only for the two or three likely changes found during clarification (pricing strategy, vehicle type, notification), and for the rest I say how I would refactor.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
New requirement Seam prepared
New vehicle type enum + SpotSize mapping, or subclass
New pricing rule PricingStrategy interface
New payment method PaymentProcessor interface + registry
Notifications Observer/listener
Persistence Repository interface with in-memory implementation

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Languages: Java, Kotlin

Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface PricingStrategy { Money fee(Duration d, VehicleType t); }
class ParkingLot {
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;
    ParkingLot(PricingStrategy pricing) { this.pricing = pricing; }
}
fun interface PricingStrategy { fun fee(d: Duration, t: VehicleType): Money }
class ParkingLot(private val pricing: PricingStrategy)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "I would rewrite it" or "just add an if".
  • Interfaces for everything.
  • Extending via inheritance when composition (strategy) is cleaner.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if it is a seam you did not prepare? -> Say the refactor: extract an interface, inject it; small classes make it cheap.
  2. How many seams? -> The 2 or 3 revealed by requirements.
  3. Enum or subclass for vehicle types? -> Enum when only data differs; subclass/strategy when behavior differs.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "use an interface". Senior: points at the exact class edits and refuses speculative seams.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Plugin systems and strategy beans are seams chosen for known variation; unknown variation is handled by refactoring when it arrives.

questions.contextHtml: Your parking lot design has SpotType {COMPACT, REGULAR, LARGE}, Spot, Level, Ticket, PricingStrategy, SpotAllocator. At minute 40 the interviewer says: "Add EV charging spots with charging time billed separately, and a weekend surge price."
questions.promptHtml: Which classes change and which stay untouched? Show the edits.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "I would add if-statements for EV in ParkingLot.park".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Can a non-EV car use an EV spot? Is charging billed by kWh or time? Does surge apply to both?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) EV is a spot type with extra state; (b) charging billing is a second pricing component; (c) weekend surge is a new pricing strategy.
  4. How I'd verify each: Walk the flow: allocate, issue ticket, compute fee. Mark each step: unchanged or changed.
  5. Root cause: N/A; it is an extension exercise.
  6. Fix: Edits:
    • SpotType: add EV; ChargingSpot extends Spot carrying charger state.
    • SpotAllocator: EV vehicles prefer EV spots (strategy tweak).
    • Pricing: a CompositePricing(List<PricingStrategy>) that sums HourlyPricing, ChargingPricing and a WeekendSurge decorator.
    • Unchanged: Ticket, Level, ParkingLot's public API.
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class WeekendSurge implements PricingStrategy {
    private final PricingStrategy base; private final Clock clock;
    public Money fee(Duration d, VehicleType t) {
        Money m = base.fee(d, t);
        return isWeekend(clock) ? m.times(1.5) : m;
    }
}
class WeekendSurge(private val base: PricingStrategy, private val clock: Clock) : PricingStrategy {
    override fun fee(d: Duration, t: VehicleType) = base.fee(d, t).let { if (isWeekend(clock)) it * 1.5 else it }
}
  1. Prevention: New rule gets a unit test with a fixed Clock.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make ParkingLot know about EV; it only talks to the allocator and pricing.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Surge differs by level? -> Pricing gets a context object (spot, time) instead of just duration and type.
  • Pricing needs charging kWh? -> Extend the fee input to a ParkingSession value.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite candidate answered "three edits, no rewrite" and named them; the interviewer ended the round early.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: if in the main class.
  • Hire: names changed and unchanged classes.
  • Strong hire: composes pricing with decorators, uses an injected clock, mentions tests.

questions.contextHtml: You are asked to compare two candidates on "design a rate limiter". Candidate A: Strategy, Factory, Observer and Singleton, five interfaces, code does not run, no edge cases, no concurrency mention. Candidate B: three classes, runs, handles first request, burst and clock edge, uses AtomicLong/lock correctly, explains how to add a sliding-window algorithm, one test. Both talked clearly.
questions.promptHtml: Who do you recommend and why? Map to a rubric.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Picks A for "more patterns".

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What level is the role? Did A attempt to run the code or have a hint to continue? Did B ignore any requirement?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The rubric has rows: requirements, modeling, principles/patterns, code quality, correctness/edges, concurrency, communication.
  4. How I'd verify each: Score each row strong/ok/weak:
Dimension            A      B
Requirements         ok     ok
Modeling             ok     strong
Patterns             weak*  strong   (*applied with no varying requirement)
Code quality         weak   ok
Correctness/edges    weak   strong
Concurrency          weak   strong
Communication        ok     strong
  1. Root cause: A optimized for decoration over correctness.
  2. Fix: Recommend B; note that A's failure was premature patterns and no running code.
  3. Prevention: For candidates: simple, correct, runnable core, then name where patterns would slot in.
  4. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not reward pattern count; patterns without a named variation read as over-engineering.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if A has strong communication and B is silent? -> Communication is its own row; it may balance but does not beat non-working code.
  • Same level? -> Check which one takes hints.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite debrief: the simpler candidate got the offer because the interviewers could run the code and the extension answer was concrete.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks A.
  • Hire: picks B with reasons.
  • Strong hire: scores per rubric row and explains why patterns without variation lose points.

questions.contextHtml: Mid-round on a parking lot, the interviewer asks: "What happens if two cars arrive at the same time and there is one spot left?" You answer, "That would be a database problem; we don't have that here," and keep coding. The interviewer repeats the question with different words 5 minutes later.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong and how should the answer go?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Defends the first answer or argues that concurrency is out of scope.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: "Do you want me to treat multiple gates as concurrent threads in this process?"
  2. Immediate mitigation: Acknowledge: "Good catch, two gates can double book; let me fix it."
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The question was a hint toward concurrency; I treated it as a challenge.
  4. How I'd verify each: Re-read my park flow: findFree then setTaken is check-then-act.
  5. Root cause: Ignoring a hint and not naming shared mutable state.
  6. Fix: Atomic claim per spot:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class Spot {
    private final AtomicBoolean taken = new AtomicBoolean(false);
    boolean tryClaim() { return taken.compareAndSet(false, true); }
}
for (Spot s : level.candidates(type)) if (s.tryClaim()) return Optional.of(new Ticket(s));
return Optional.empty();
class Spot { private val taken = AtomicBoolean(false); fun tryClaim() = taken.compareAndSet(false, true) }
  1. Prevention: At clarification, list shared state and gates; say the thread-safety stance up front.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not make everything synchronized or insist concurrency is out of scope.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why not a global lock? -> Simplest and correct, but serializes all gates.
  • How do you test? -> 100 threads, 10 spots, assert exactly 10 successes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite candidate fixed the race in two minutes after a hint and was scored higher than another who defended the original code.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: argues or ignores.
  • Hire: acknowledges and fixes.
  • Strong hire: fixes with per-spot claim, names the trade-off and offers a test.

questions.promptHtml: How do you communicate decisions during an LLD round, and what do you do when you get stuck or find your own mistake?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Interviewers grade communication separately and weigh recovery heavily: it predicts how you behave in design reviews.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Each decision gets one sentence: choice, reason, alternative ("Map<String,Ticket> for O(1) lookup; the alternative is a list scan, O(n)"). If stuck, I name what I am stuck on, pick one option with its trade-off, continue, and offer to revisit. If I find a mistake, I say so and fix it quickly. I finish with a dry run using concrete values.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Dry run example:

park(car KA-01) -> Level 0 free car spot #12 -> Ticket T-1 (entry 10:00)
unpark(T-1) at 12:30 -> 3 hours (rounded up) x Rs 40 = Rs 120

Recovery protocol: (1) state the problem, (2) decide, (3) move on, (4) revisit in the last minutes. Silence and defending a flawed choice are the failure modes.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Long unexplained pauses.
  • Defending a flawed choice.
  • Vague dry runs ("it would work").

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What if you do not know an API? -> Say the behavior you need and write a plausible signature, flagged as such.
  2. What if the interviewer disagrees with a choice? -> Ask why, weigh it, adjust or defend with a trade-off.
  3. What if you realize the model is wrong at minute 35? -> Patch minimally, state the cost of a full fix.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: works quietly. Senior: narrates trade-offs, takes hints, recovers explicitly.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: The same narration is what makes design review comments useful and incident bridges productive.

questions.contextHtml: At minute 38 of a library-management round, while doing the dry run, you notice Library.checkout() allows borrowing an already-borrowed copy: you modelled Book and Copy as one class, so there is no per-copy state. There are 7 minutes left and 200 lines written.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Hides it or restarts the model in a panic.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: "Should I do a minimal patch or the cleaner model split? I have 7 minutes."
  2. Immediate mitigation: Say it: "Dry run shows I conflated Book and Copy; a copy can be borrowed twice."
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) split Book (title, isbn) and BookCopy (id, status); (b) add a borrowed flag on the existing class; (c) leave it and discuss.
  4. How I'd verify each: Count the call sites: how many reference Book.available?
  5. Root cause: Skipped the noun/owner check in the entity step.
  6. Fix: The minimal patch in 3 minutes:
Languages: Java · Kotlin
class BookCopy {
    private final String id; private final Book book; private boolean borrowed;
    synchronized boolean tryBorrow() { if (borrowed) return false; borrowed = true; return true; }
}
class BookCopy(val id: String, val book: Book) {
    private var borrowed = false
    @Synchronized fun tryBorrow(): Boolean { if (borrowed) return false; borrowed = true; return true }
}

Then re-run the dry run with two copies of one title. 7. Prevention: In the entity step ask "what has its own state?" for every noun. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not do a full rewrite with 7 minutes left; I would state what a complete fix looks like.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Interviewer asks why you did not catch it earlier? -> Honest answer: I merged two nouns; here is the check I now do.
  • Concurrency on tryBorrow? -> Synchronized or CAS per copy.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite interviewer wrote "recovered gracefully" in the debrief for exactly this case.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: hides it or panics.
  • Hire: says it and patches.
  • Strong hire: patches, re-runs the dry run, explains the entity-check habit.

questions.contextHtml: In a ride-sharing LLD round you proposed RideMatchingStrategy, PricingStrategy, NotificationObserver, PaymentFactory, DriverRepository and AuditLogger. The interviewer says: "That is six abstractions for a 45-minute problem, and some have one implementation. Justify them." You have 15 minutes left.
questions.promptHtml: Which do you keep and which do you cut? How do you defend the choice?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Defends all six as "best practice", or deletes all and says it is simple.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which changes did we agree are likely? (matching algorithm and surge pricing were named in the requirements.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Triage by "can I name the second variant or a test that needs it?"
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Keep Matching (nearest vs rating-based) and Pricing (normal vs surge): both were named. Keep DriverRepository as an interface with an in-memory implementation because tests need it. Cut PaymentFactory (payments out of scope), AuditLogger (a plain logger) and NotificationObserver (mention as a future seam).
  4. How I'd verify each: Look at the requirement list from minute 5.
  5. Root cause: Seams built for imagined change.
  6. Fix: Show the reduced model and say: "For notifications I would add an observer interface when a second channel is requested; it is a small change because Ride already emits state changes."
Languages: Java · Kotlin
interface RideMatchingStrategy { Optional<Driver> match(Rider r, List<Driver> free); }
interface PricingStrategy { Money fare(Ride r); }
fun interface RideMatchingStrategy { fun match(r: Rider, free: List<Driver>): Driver? }
fun interface PricingStrategy { fun fare(r: Ride): Money }
  1. Prevention: Prepare seams for the 2 or 3 changes the clarifying questions revealed.
  2. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not get defensive; I would show I can justify with the named variation.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Interviewer asks for the notification channel right now? -> Add the interface and one implementation in 2 minutes; that shows cutting was cheap.
  • Is a repository over-engineering? -> It pays for itself in tests.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite candidate cut four of six abstractions mid-interview and was praised for judgment.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: defends all or removes all.
  • Hire: keeps the named-variation seams.
  • Strong hire: criteria-based triage plus a refactoring story for the cut ones.
